paper.title: Hydrogen Clathrate Structures in Rare Earth Hydrides at High Pressures: Possible Route to Room-Temperature Superconductivity
paper.abstract: Room-temperature superconductivity has been a long-held dream and an area of intensive research. Recent experimental findings of superconductivity at 200 K in highly compressed hydrogen (H) sulfides have demonstrated the potential for achieving room-temperature superconductivity in compressed H-rich materials. We report first-principles structure searches for stable H-rich clathrate structures in rare earth hydrides at high pressures. The peculiarity of these structures lies in the emergence of unusual H cages with stoichiometries H 24 , H 29 , and H 32 , in which H atoms are weakly covalently bonded to one another, with rare earth atoms occupying the centers of the cages. We have found that high-temperature superconductivity is closely associated with H clathrate structures, with large H-derived electronic densities of states at the Fermi level and strong electron-phonon coupling related to the stretching and rocking motions of H atoms within the cages. Strikingly, a yttrium (Y) H 32 clathrate structure of stoichiometry YH 10 is predicted to be a potential room-temperature superconductor with an estimated T c of up to 303 K at 400 GPa, as derived by direct solution of the Eliashberg equation.
paper.summary:
1. First-principles exploration of compressed rare-earth hydrides, including Sc, Y, La, Ce, and Pr systems, using CALYPSO searches and independent random-search confirmation of selected structures identifies hydrogen clathrates across the studied systems, extending the known H24 cages in REH6 to larger H29 and H32 cages in REH9 and REH10, respectively.
2. Formation-enthalpy comparisons establish composition-dependent stability, while quasiharmonic free-energy calculations show that temperature can stabilize YH10 above 1000 K; the structurally analogous LaH10 is unstable against LaH3 and LaH11 at 200 GPa, emphasizing that promising superconducting structures need not be the zero-temperature thermodynamic ground state.
3. Electronic-structure and linear-response calculations associate superconductivity with substantial hydrogen-derived Fermi-level states and strong coupling to cage stretching and rocking vibrations, with reported electron–phonon coupling parameters of 4.42 for YH9 at 150 GPa and 2.41 for YH10 at 400 GPa, rather than with hydrogen content alone.
4. Direct Eliashberg calculations predict transition temperatures of 276 K for YH9 at 150 GPa, 303 K for YH10 at 400 GPa, and 288 K for LaH10 at 200 GPa using a Coulomb pseudopotential of 0.1, identifying rare-earth hydrogen clathrates as candidates for room-temperature superconductivity under compression and motivating future high-pressure synthesis rather than reporting experimental confirmation.

evidence.quote: Here we report an extensive exploration of the highpressure phase diagrams of RE (Sc, Y, La, Ce, Pr, etc.) hydrides, focusing on H-rich species by performing swarmintelligence based CALYPso [33,34] structure searches.

methodology: First-principles structure prediction using swarm-intelligence CALYPSO searches and independent ab initio random structure searching for selected clathrates.
Density-functional-theory local optimization and pressure-dependent structural relaxation using VASP or CASTEP.
Formation-enthalpy and convex-hull analysis of hydride phase stability.
Quasiharmonic free-energy calculations using Phonopy to examine temperature-dependent stability.
Linear-response phonon and electron-phonon coupling calculations using Quantum ESPRESSO.
Direct solution of the Eliashberg equation to predict superconducting transition temperatures.
Electronic band-structure, density-of-states, electron-localization, and chemical-bonding analyses.
paper.knowledge_graph_title: Predicted Room-Temperature Superconductivity in YH10 and Hydrogen Clathrates of Rare-Earth Hydrides
paper.key_finding: First-principles searches predict rare-earth hydride clathrates built from H24, H29, and H32 cages, with superconductivity arising from hydrogen-derived Fermi-level states and strong electron-phonon coupling involving cage vibrations; temperature-stabilized YH10 is predicted to reach a superconducting transition temperature of up to 303 K at 400 GPa.
paper.research_motivation:
1. Increasing hydrogen content alone does not reliably increase superconducting transition temperatures because H2-like molecular units can remove electronic states from the Fermi level and undermine favorable electron-phonon coupling.
2. The authors seek binary hydrides with greater hydrogen content than CaH6 and YH6 but without molecular hydrogen, targeting rare-earth metals whose electron donation could support more hydrogen-rich extended lattices.
builds_on: Previously predicted H24 clathrate cages in CaH6 and YH6 provide the structural and electron-donation design precedent for seeking more hydrogen-rich cages.

Here we report an extensive exploration of the highpressure phase diagrams of RE (Sc, Y, La, Ce, Pr, etc.) hydrides, focusing on H-rich species by performing swarmintelligence based CALYPso [33,34] structure searches. Besides the known \mathrm { H } _ { 2 4 } cage structure in \mathrm { R E H } _ { 6 } , H-rich \mathrm { H } _ { 2 9 } and \mathrm { H } _ { 3 2 } cage structures were predicted in \mathrm { R E H _ { 9 } } and \mathrm { R E H _ { 1 0 } } hydrides. Among them, the \mathrm { H } _ { 3 2 } cage structure in the temperature-stabilized \mathrm{NH_{10}} clathrate is predicted to be a potential room-temperature superconductor with a T _ { c } of up to 303 K at 400 GPa, as derived by direct solution of the Eliashberg equation [37].

evidences.quote: FIG. 4. Calculated electronic DOS of H at the Fermi level ( N _ { E f } ) per \mathrm { \AA } ^ { 3 } (top panel), the EPC parameter λ (middle panel), and T _ { c } (bottom panel) of various clathrate structures at high pressures. The pressure values chosen within their stable pressure ranges of the phases are 300, 400, 120,150, 400, 100, 50, 100, 200, and 100 GPa for \mathrm { S c H _ { 6 } } , ScH9, \mathrm { Y H _ { 6 } } , YH9, YH10, LaH6, LaH9, CeH9, \mathrm { C e H _ { 1 0 } } , and \mathrm { P r H } _ { 9 } , respectively.

Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

pressure_value_gpa.quote: Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. point (Fig. S14 [38]), the large λ values are mainly associated with in-plane stretching, in-plane rocking, and out-of-plane rocking vibrations of H clathrate cages (Fig. S15 [38]). The Eliashberg equation [37] gives a better description of systems with strong electron-phonon coupling for \lambda > 1 . 5 We have therefore used the Eliashberg equation to predict superconductivity in the clathrate structures using the calculated logarithmic average frequency ( \omega _ { \mathrm { l o g } } ) and typical Coulomb pseudopotential parameters ( \mu \% ) from 0.1 to 0.13, The resulting T _ { c } values are 276 K (253 K for \mu^{*} = 0.13 and 303 K (287 K for \mu^{*} = 0.13 using \mu^{*} = 0. 1 for \mathrm { Y H } _ { 9 } at 150 GPa and \mathrm{NH_{10}} at 400 GPa, respectively.The calculated T _ { c } of \mathrm { L a H _ { 1 0 } } reaches 288 K using \mu ^ { * } = 0 . 1 at 200 GPa. We also investigated potential superconductivity in other clathrate structures (Fig. 4) and predicted T _ { c } values for \mathrm { S c H _ { 6 } } and \mathrm { S c H _ { 9 } } as high as ~150 K, although for L \mathrm{aH_{9},CeH_{9},CeH_{10}} and \mathrm { P r H } _ { 9 } they are much lower at < 5 6 \mathrm { K } ( \mathrm { F i g . } 4 ) due to the introduction of much heavier elements which reduce BCS superconductivity.

The phonon calculations were carried out by using supercell approach [17] as implemented in the phonopy code [18]. All structures of RE-H compounds are demonstrated to be dynamically stable in their stable pressure ranges by phonon calculations. The EPC parameter λ of the stable compounds are calculated within the framework of linear response theory through the Quantum-ESPRESSO code [19].

point (Fig. S14 [38]), the large λ values are mainly associated with in-plane stretching, in-plane rocking, and out-of-plane rocking vibrations of H clathrate cages (Fig. S15 [38]). Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

evidences.quote: FIG. 4. Calculated electronic DOS of H at the Fermi level ( N _ { E f } ) per \mathrm { \AA } ^ { 3 } (top panel), the EPC parameter λ (middle panel), and T _ { c } (bottom panel) of various clathrate structures at high pressures. The pressure values chosen within their stable pressure ranges of the phases are 300, 400, 120,150, 400, 100, 50, 100, 200, and 100 GPa for \mathrm { S c H _ { 6 } } , ScH9, \mathrm { Y H _ { 6 } } , YH9, YH10, LaH6, LaH9, CeH9, \mathrm { C e H _ { 1 0 } } , and \mathrm { P r H } _ { 9 } , respectively.

The H clathrate structures of \mathrm { R E H _ { 6 } ,   R E H _ { 9 } } , and \mathrm { R E H _ { 1 0 } } are metallic as seen from the calculated electronic band structures and densities of states (Figs. S13 and S14 [38]). The electronic density of states at the Fermi level is typically large and is dominated by the contribution from H atoms. To examine potential superconductivity in the clathrate structures, lattice phonons and electron-phonon coupling (EPC) calculations were carried out using linear response theory [68]. Encouragingly, the resulting EPC parameters, \lambda , of \mathrm { \underline { { Y H } } } _ { 9 } and \mathrm{NH_{10}} are quite large and reach values of 4.42 and 2.41 at 150 and 400 GPa, respectively. Besides the H-derived high density of states at the Fermi level that is associated with a van Hove singularity at the Γ

point (Fig. S14 [38]), the large λ values are mainly associated with in-plane stretching, in-plane rocking, and out-of-plane rocking vibrations of H clathrate cages (Fig. S15 [38]). The Eliashberg equation [37] gives a better description of systems with strong electron-phonon coupling for \lambda > 1 . 5 We have therefore used the Eliashberg equation to predict superconductivity in the clathrate structures using the calculated logarithmic average frequency ( \omega _ { \mathrm { l o g } } ) and typical Coulomb pseudopotential parameters ( \mu \% ) from 0.1 to 0.13, The resulting T _ { c } values are 276 K (253 K for \mu^{*} = 0.13 and 303 K (287 K for \mu^{*} = 0.13 using \mu^{*} = 0. 1 for \mathrm { Y H } _ { 9 } at 150 GPa and \mathrm{NH_{10}} at 400 GPa, respectively.The calculated T _ { c } of \mathrm { L a H _ { 1 0 } } reaches 288 K using \mu ^ { * } = 0 . 1 at 200 GPa. We also investigated potential superconductivity in other clathrate structures (Fig. 4) and predicted T _ { c } values for \mathrm { S c H _ { 6 } } and \mathrm { S c H _ { 9 } } as high as ~150 K, although for L \mathrm{aH_{9},CeH_{9},CeH_{10}} and \mathrm { P r H } _ { 9 } they are much lower at < 5 6 \mathrm { K } ( \mathrm { F i g . } 4 ) due to the introduction of much heavier elements which reduce BCS superconductivity.

The phonon calculations were carried out by using supercell approach [17] as implemented in the phonopy code [18]. All structures of RE-H compounds are demonstrated to be dynamically stable in their stable pressure ranges by phonon calculations. The EPC parameter λ of the stable compounds are calculated within the framework of linear response theory through the Quantum-ESPRESSO code [19].

point (Fig. S14 [38]), the large λ values are mainly associated with in-plane stretching, in-plane rocking, and out-of-plane rocking vibrations of H clathrate cages (Fig. S15 [38]). The Eliashberg equation [37] gives a better description of systems with strong electron-phonon coupling for \lambda > 1 . 5 We have therefore used the Eliashberg equation to predict superconductivity in the clathrate structures using the calculated logarithmic average frequency ( \omega _ { \mathrm { l o g } } ) and typical Coulomb pseudopotential parameters ( \mu \% ) from 0.1 to 0.13, The resulting T _ { c } values are 276 K (253 K for \mu^{*} = 0.13 and 303 K (287 K for \mu^{*} = 0.13 using \mu^{*} = 0. 1 for \mathrm { Y H } _ { 9 } at 150 GPa and \mathrm{NH_{10}} at 400 GPa, respectively.The calculated T _ { c } of \mathrm { L a H _ { 1 0 } } reaches 288 K using \mu ^ { * } = 0 . 1 at 200 GPa. The phonon calculations were carried out by using supercell approach [17] as implemented in the phonopy code [18]. The EPC parameter λ of the stable compounds are calculated within the framework of linear response theory through the Quantum-ESPRESSO code [19].

point (Fig. S14 [38]), the large λ values are mainly associated with in-plane stretching, in-plane rocking, and out-of-plane rocking vibrations of H clathrate cages (Fig. S15 [38]). The Eliashberg equation [37] gives a better description of systems with strong electron-phonon coupling for \lambda > 1 . 5 We have therefore used the Eliashberg equation to predict superconductivity in the clathrate structures using the calculated logarithmic average frequency ( \omega _ { \mathrm { l o g } } ) and typical Coulomb pseudopotential parameters ( \mu \% ) from 0.1 to 0.13, The resulting T _ { c } values are 276 K (253 K for \mu^{*} = 0.13 and 303 K (287 K for \mu^{*} = 0.13 using \mu^{*} = 0. 1 for \mathrm { Y H } _ { 9 } at 150 GPa and \mathrm{NH_{10}} at 400 GPa, respectively.The calculated T _ { c } of \mathrm { L a H _ { 1 0 } } reaches 288 K using \mu ^ { * } = 0 . 1 at 200 GPa. We also investigated potential superconductivity in other clathrate structures (Fig. 4) and predicted T _ { c } values for \mathrm { S c H _ { 6 } } and \mathrm { S c H _ { 9 } } as high as ~150 K, although for L \mathrm{aH_{9},CeH_{9},CeH_{10}} and \mathrm { P r H } _ { 9 } they are much lower at < 5 6 \mathrm { K } ( \mathrm { F i g . } 4 ) due to the introduction of much heavier elements which reduce BCS superconductivity.

The phonon calculations were carried out by using supercell approach [17] as implemented in the phonopy code [18]. All structures of RE-H compounds are demonstrated to be dynamically stable in their stable pressure ranges by phonon calculations. The EPC parameter λ of the stable compounds are calculated within the framework of linear response theory through the Quantum-ESPRESSO code [19].

Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

we plotted enthalpy curves of CeH2 phases in two different ways in Fig. S38. The solid and hollow enthalpy curves are calculated from DFT within the GGA and GGA+U functionals respectively The phase transition from Fm-3m to P6/mmm phase is found within both of these two different functionals, despite a shift of 7 GPa regarding the phase transition pressure. Such shift is reasonable since GGA+U functional is well known to raise enthalpies of hydirdes due to additional filed. The order of stability of Ce hydrides is important for its phase diagram at high pressure. We therefore neglect the Hubbard U correction in our calculations of rare earth hydrides.

we plotted enthalpy curves of CeH2 phases in two different ways in Fig. S38. The solid and hollow enthalpy curves are calculated from DFT within the GGA and GGA+U functionals respectively The phase transition from Fm-3m to P6/mmm phase is found within both of these two different functionals, despite a shift of 7 GPa regarding the phase transition pressure. Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

sources.quote: Once we have the predicted structures at hand, we then optimized a number of low-enthalpy structures at a higher accuracy as a function of pressure using either VASP or CASTEP method. The plane wave basis set was constructed using the energy cutoff of 800 eV in all calculations, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a k-point resolution of 2 \pi \times 0 . 0 3 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } . This usually gives total enthalpies well converged within ~ 1 meV/atom. The PAW potentials [13] are adopted for Sc, Y, Ce, and H in Sc-H, Y-H, and Ce-H systems for VASP calculations. While On The Fly (OTF) potentials are adopted for La, Pr and H in La-H and Pr-H systems for CASTEP calculations. The exchange-correlation functional was described using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof [14] of generalized gradient approximation [15]

metadata.title: Hydrogen Clathrate Structures in Rare Earth Hydrides at High Pressures: Possible Route to Room-Temperature Superconductivity
metadata.abstract: Room-temperature superconductivity has been a long-held dream and an area of intensive research. Recent experimental findings of superconductivity at 200 K in highly compressed hydrogen (H) sulfides have demonstrated the potential for achieving room-temperature superconductivity in compressed H-rich materials. We report first-principles structure searches for stable H-rich clathrate structures in rare earth hydrides at high pressures. The peculiarity of these structures lies in the emergence of unusual H cages with stoichiometries H 24 , H 29 , and H 32 , in which H atoms are weakly covalently bonded to one another, with rare earth atoms occupying the centers of the cages. We have found that high-temperature superconductivity is closely associated with H clathrate structures, with large H-derived electronic densities of states at the Fermi level and strong electron-phonon coupling related to the stretching and rocking motions of H atoms within the cages. Strikingly, a yttrium (Y) H 32 clathrate structure of stoichiometry YH 10 is predicted to be a potential room-temperature superconductor with an estimated T c of up to 303 K at 400 GPa, as derived by direct solution of the Eliashberg equation.

authors.text: Feng Peng | Ying Sun | Chris J Pickard | Richard J Needs | Qiang Wu | Yanming Ma

research_motivation:
1. Increasing hydrogen content alone does not reliably increase superconducting transition temperatures because H2-like molecular units can remove electronic states from the Fermi level and undermine favorable electron-phonon coupling.
2. The authors seek binary hydrides with greater hydrogen content than CaH6 and YH6 but without molecular hydrogen, targeting rare-earth metals whose electron donation could support more hydrogen-rich extended lattices.

Here we report an extensive exploration of the highpressure phase diagrams of RE (Sc, Y, La, Ce, Pr, etc.) hydrides, focusing on H-rich species by performing swarmintelligence based CALYPso [33,34] structure searches. Some of the key clathrate structures were subsequently confirmed using the ab initio random structure searching approach [35,36]. Our structure searches revealed that H clathrate structures could be formed in all of the RE hydrides studied. Besides the known \mathrm { H } _ { 2 4 } cage structure in \mathrm { R E H } _ { 6 } , H-rich \mathrm { H } _ { 2 9 } and \mathrm { H } _ { 3 2 } cage structures were predicted in \mathrm { R E H _ { 9 } } and \mathrm { R E H _ { 1 0 } } hydrides. Among them, the \mathrm { H } _ { 3 2 } cage structure in the temperature-stabilized \mathrm{NH_{10}} clathrate is predicted to be a potential room-temperature superconductor with a T _ { c } of up to 303 K at 400 GPa, as derived by direct solution of the Eliashberg equation [37].

evidences.quote: Structure searches for rare earth (RE) hydrides of REHx (x = 1 - 12 and 13-24) with simulation cells ranging from one to four formula units were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, and 400 GPa. Our CALYPSO structural searches focus mainly on the REHx (x = 2-12) stoichiometries, Ab Initio Random Structure Searching (AIRSS) [10] calculations were also employed to confirm some of our key clathrate structures, while some H-richer stoichiometries REHx (x =13-24) were also considered in the AIRSS approach [10]. Each generation contained 50 structures, and structures in the first generation were produced randomly with symmetry constraints. All the generated structures are optimized to their local minima by using DFT calculations. Here, almost all geometrical optimization calculations are performed by using PAW potentials and VASP code [11]. There are two exceptions on La hydrides and Pr hydrides, where the geometrical optimizations are performed by OTF potentials and CASTEP code [12] since PAW potentials of La and Pr are invalid to be used at high pressure as tested. During structure evolution, 60% of structures in the first generation with lower enthalpies are selected to produce the structures in the next generation by PSO. 40% of the structures in the new generation are randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique of bond characterization matrix is applied to produce structures, so that identical structures are strictly forbidden. These procedures significantly enhance the diversity of structures, which is crucial for the searching efficiency of algorithm. The local optimizations are performed by use of the conjugate gradients method and the criteria of the enthalpy change is 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }   \mathrm { e V } per atom. For most of the cases, the structure searches reach the convergence after 50 generations covering about 2500 structures.

title.text: Hydrogen Clathrate Structures in Rare Earth Hydrides at High Pressures: Possible Route to Room-Temperature Superconductivity

abstract.text: Room-temperature superconductivity has been a long-held dream and an area of intensive research. Recent experimental findings of superconductivity at 200 K in highly compressed hydrogen (H) sulfides have demonstrated the potential for achieving room-temperature superconductivity in compressed H-rich materials. We report first-principles structure searches for stable H-rich clathrate structures in rare earth hydrides at high pressures. The peculiarity of these structures lies in the emergence of unusual H cages with stoichiometries H 24 , H 29 , and H 32 , in which H atoms are weakly covalently bonded to one another, with rare earth atoms occupying the centers of the cages. We have found that high-temperature superconductivity is closely associated with H clathrate structures, with large H-derived electronic densities of states at the Fermi level and strong electron-phonon coupling related to the stretching and rocking motions of H atoms within the cages. Strikingly, a yttrium (Y) H 32 clathrate structure of stoichiometry YH 10 is predicted to be a potential room-temperature superconductor with an estimated T c of up to 303 K at 400 GPa, as derived by direct solution of the Eliashberg equation.

bibliography_conflicts.selected_value: Room-temperature superconductivity has been a long-held dream and an area of intensive research. Recent experimental findings of superconductivity at 200 K in highly compressed hydrogen (H) sulfides have demonstrated the potential for achieving room-temperature superconductivity in compressed H-rich materials. We report first-principles structure searches for stable H-rich clathrate structures in rare earth hydrides at high pressures. The peculiarity of these structures lies in the emergence of unusual H cages with stoichiometries H 24 , H 29 , and H 32 , in which H atoms are weakly covalently bonded to one another, with rare earth atoms occupying the centers of the cages. We have found that high-temperature superconductivity is closely associated with H clathrate structures, with large H-derived electronic densities of states at the Fermi level and strong electron-phonon coupling related to the stretching and rocking motions of H atoms within the cages. Strikingly, a yttrium (Y) H 32 clathrate structure of stoichiometry YH 10 is predicted to be a potential room-temperature superconductor with an estimated T c of up to 303 K at 400 GPa, as derived by direct solution of the Eliashberg equation.

parsing_conflicts.selected_text: Here we report an extensive exploration of the highpressure phase diagrams of RE (Sc, Y, La, Ce, Pr, etc.) hydrides, focusing on H-rich species by performing swarmintelligence based CALYPso [33,34] structure searches. Some of the key clathrate structures were subsequently confirmed using the ab initio random structure searching approach [35,36]. Our structure searches revealed that H clathrate structures could be formed in all of the RE hydrides studied. Besides the known \mathrm { H } _ { 2 4 } cage structure in \mathrm { R E H } _ { 6 } , H-rich \mathrm { H } _ { 2 9 } and \mathrm { H } _ { 3 2 } cage structures were predicted in \mathrm { R E H _ { 9 } } and \mathrm { R E H _ { 1 0 } } hydrides. Among them, the \mathrm { H } _ { 3 2 } cage structure in the temperature-stabilized \mathrm{NH_{10}} clathrate is predicted to be a potential room-temperature superconductor with a T _ { c } of up to 303 K at 400 GPa, as derived by direct solution of the Eliashberg equation [37].

parsing_conflicts.selected_text: Our extensive structure searches for RE \mathrm { ( R E = S c , Y , } La, \operatorname { C e } , and Pr) hydrides have revealed the appearance of stable clathrate structures in \mathrm { R E H } _ { 6 } , \mathrm { R E H } _ { 9 } , and \mathrm { R E H _ { 1 0 } } These structures have extended our searches into other REs \mathrm { ( R E = N d , } , Pm, Sm, Eu, Gd, Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm, \mathrm { Y b } . and Lu) hydrides using density-functional-theory calculations and substituting the RE elements into the known \mathrm { R E H } _ { 6 } , REH9, and \mathrm { R E H _ { 1 0 } } structures (Supplemental Figs. { \scriptstyle { \mathrm { S } } 1 6 - { \mathrm { S } } 2 7 } [38]). Our results show that clathrate structures often emerge in these RE hydrides. Stabilization of clathrate structures using RE hydrides at high pressures might, therefore, be a widespread phenomenon. Two families of binary hydrides ( \mathbf { i . e . } , nonmetals with high electronegativity and metal hydrides) are promising candidates for high-T _ { c } superconductivity. For nonmetal hydrides in which H is able to form covalent bonds with nonmetallic elements, the three-dimensional covalently bonded H structure appears only in the high-T \mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { S } [14] and \mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { S e } [69] materials.
